title: Willie Mosconi: 15 world titles and the 526
t: Willie Mosconi: 15 world titles and the 526
description:
Willie Mosconi (1913-1993) won 15 world straight-pool championships and, on March 19-20, 1954, in Springfield, Ohio, ran 526 consecutive balls — witnessed, affidavit-signed, never broken. The run took over two hours; he reportedly quit only because he was tired.

Mosconi was pool's first true professional star: handsome, precise, and unbeatable for two decades. The Mosconi Cup bears his name.

title: Ralph Greenleaf: the 1920s king
description:
Ralph Greenleaf (1899-1950) won 20 world championships between 1919 and 1937, dominating pool's first golden age. A vaudeville performer as well as a player, he brought showmanship to the championship table.

His rivalry with Willie Mosconi bridged two eras; his 20 world titles remain among the most ever.

title: Rudolf "Minnesota Fats" Wanderone: the hustler myth
t: Rudolf "Minnesota Fats" Wanderone: the hustler myth
description:
Rudolf Wanderone (1913-1996) claimed — loudly, endlessly — to be the real 'Minnesota Fats' of Walter Tevis's novel and The Hustler. Whether or not he was, he became pool's great character: the fast-talking, big-eating hustler who'd play anyone, anywhere.

Fats never won a major tournament. He didn't need to — he won immortality instead.

description:
Irving 'the Deacon' Crane (1913-2001) won world titles across four decades with a precise, gentlemanly game. His nickname came from his quiet, almost clerical demeanor at the table.

Crane's longevity — competing at the top into his 60s — set the template for the modern professional career.

Lassiter proved the road player's creed: the tournament is the advertisement; the money game is the business.

description:

Reyes learned in money games; his imagination at the table has never been matched.

At his best, no one in history ran racks faster.

Archer's consistency made him the backbone of early Mosconi Cup USA teams.

Mizerak proved a champion could also be the sport's best salesman.

Every woman who plays professionally today walks a road Katsura opened.

Fifteen titles, zero defeats — the most unassailable record in cue sports.

t: Walter Lindrum: the Don Bradman of billiards
description:

His 1932 world-record break took nearly three hours.

title: Steve Davis: the 1980s
description:
Steve Davis (b. 1957) won 6 World Snooker Championships in the 1980s, making snooker Britain's biggest TV sport. His methodical, almost robotic game earned the 'Interesting' nickname ironically — he was box office.

Davis's 1985 final against Dennis Taylor — decided on the last black at 12:23 a.m. — drew 18.5 million viewers, Britain's biggest post-midnight audience ever.

t: The champion's toolkit: break, safety, and nerve
description:
What separates champions: a break that controls the table, safeties that strangle opponents, and nerve that holds at hill-hill. Reyes' kicks, Strickland's firepower, Davis's method, O'Sullivan's genius — different expressions of the same mastery: the cue ball obeying thought.

Technique can be taught; temperament is the mystery.

definitions.World champion: Winner of a recognized world championship (WPA, World Snooker, or historic bodies).
definitions.Ranking title: A professional tournament win counting toward official rankings.
definitions.Century break: A snooker break of 100+ points in one visit.
definitions.Maximum break: A 147 in snooker — the perfect break.
definitions.High run: The most consecutive balls pocketed in straight pool; Mosconi's 526 is the legend.
definitions.Mosconi Cup: The annual Europe-vs-USA team event, pool's Ryder Cup, since 1994.

source: Billiards Congress of America Hall of Fame; World Pool Association; World Snooker Tour records
